title: Start from a template
description: List the built-in templates with kikx presets, create a whole project with kikx setup, then explore and change the files you now own.
outcomes: Read the template list from kikx presets
Create a full project in one command with kikx setup
Find your way around the files a template writes
Know that the files are yours, and how to re-render one component

checks.retimed: You re-rendered {roleName} with {timezoneSet} and the force option

recap: kikx presets lists the built-in templates, with how many components each one adds.
kikx setup creates kikx.toml and writes every file of the template in one go.
The files land in the output folder, laid out the way the tools expect them.
From then on the files are yours: edit them, commit them, kikx never syncs them back.
Re-rendering one component with the force option replaces just its files, edits included.

steps.intro: Starting from nothing is fine, but kikx also ships templates: complete projects you can start from in one command.
steps.templateLine: Each template has a name, a title, the number of components it adds and a short description. We'll use {template}.
steps.pick: These are the same templates as on the home page of the app, so you can start in either place.
steps.setup: Your turn. Click the terminal, type kikx setup {template} and press Enter.
steps.initialized: One command created the project and wrote every file of the template into the output folder.
steps.tree: Here they are: infrastructure code, an inventory, group vars, a role and playbooks, all laid out the way Ansible and Terraform expect.
steps.openToml: kikx.toml takes its settings from the template.
steps.tomlName: Even the project name comes from it. Change it here whenever you like.
steps.openSite: site.yml is the entry point of the Ansible side.
steps.siteLine: Each import_playbook line runs a playbook in order.
steps.openInventory: The inventory lists the servers the playbooks talk to.
steps.inventoryLine: The template ships an example host, {host}. Replace it with your own server before you run anything.
steps.ls: Files are plain files on disk, so the usual tools work, like ls.
steps.own: This is the key idea: kikx vendors files. Once written, they belong to you and kikx never touches them again on its own.
steps.editing: To change something, edit the file in your editor. Or ask kikx to render one component again with new values.
steps.retime: Your turn. Re-render the common role with a new timezone: kikx add {roleComponent} {flagName} {roleName} {flagSet} {timezoneSet} {flagForce}.
steps.overwritten: With {flagForce}, kikx replaces the role's files with a fresh render.
steps.timezoneLine: The new timezone is in the tasks.
steps.force: Use {flagForce} with care: it replaces the whole file, so any hand edits in it are gone. Commit first and the diff shows what changed.
steps.done: You started a full project from a template, found your way around it and changed it. Next, see how the app and the CLI work together.
steps.openTerraform: Start with the servers. The Terraform file creates the droplet the rest of the project configures.
steps.regionLine: Its settings came from the template, like the region {region}. Change them to suit your account.
steps.openGroupVars: group_vars holds settings shared by every host in a group, loaded by Ansible because of the file name.
steps.groupVarLine: Here the template sets {groupVar} for the app group.
steps.openPlaybook: The playbook says which hosts to configure and which roles to run on them.
steps.playbookLine: It runs the {roleName} role, which the template also wrote under roles.
steps.cat: And cat prints a file, here the Ansible config that ties the inventory and the roles together.
